title: Inventions and Inventors
description: Ten informative stories about inventions and the many people behind them: printing, the light bulb, the Wright brothers' wind tunnel, Hedy Lamarr's frequency hopping, the zipper, the microwave oven, Grace Hopper's compiler, the shipping container, refrigeration and the oldest inventions of all.

lessons.title: Many Hands Behind the Printed Page
lessons.summary: Printing with movable type grew from Bi Sheng and Wang Zhen in China, through Korean metal type, to Gutenberg in Mainz.
lessons.text:
Ask who invented printing with movable type, and most people will name Johannes Gutenberg. The real story is longer, and it begins in China about four hundred years before him.

Around 1040, a craftsman named Bi Sheng made small blocks of baked clay, each carrying a single raised character. He set them in an iron frame, inked them and pressed paper against them. Afterward, the blocks could be used again. It was a new paradigm: instead of carving a whole page into one block of wood, a printer built each page from pieces that could move.

Wang Zhen, an official under the Yuan dynasty, which ruled China from 1271 to 1368, had more than 60,000 characters carved in wood. He kept them on large round tables that turned, so that a worker could sit still and let the characters come to him. The word Yuan, by the way, is also the name of Chinese money today. In Korea, printers went further and cast type in metal. A Buddhist book called Jikji, printed with metal type in 1377, is the oldest such book that survives.

Gutenberg, a goldsmith in the German city of Mainz, probably knew nothing of these Asian methods, yet around 1450 he reached the same paradigm by his own route. He combined several ideas into one system: a hand mold for casting thousands of identical metal letters, an ink based on oil that stuck to metal, and a press adapted from the presses used for making wine. His letters were designed to imitate the handwriting of the monks who copied books by hand, because readers trusted what looked familiar. The pages imitated handwritten books so closely that artists were later paid to paint an ornament at the start of each chapter, and the richest copies have ornaments of gold.

Gutenberg printed the Bible in its entirety, in some 180 copies. Printing a book in its entirety was expensive, and his partner Johann Fust had lent him large sums of money. In 1455, Fust took him to court and took over much of the workshop. Did Fust betray Gutenberg? Some historians think so; others say that asking for your money back is not the same as betraying a friend.

The printers' world also left its mark on our terminology. Type was kept in wooden cases, with capital letters in the upper case and small letters in the lower case. That terminology survives every time we capitalize a name, or a phone asks whether we want to capitalize a word.

Lastly, it is worth remembering how wide the circle of credit is. Bi Sheng, Wang Zhen, the Korean printers and Gutenberg all solved the same problem in their own ways, and each of them deserves a place in the story.

Questions:
What did Bi Sheng make his type from?
He made it from small blocks of baked clay, each carrying a single character.
Why did Gutenberg's letters imitate the handwriting of monks?
Readers trusted what looked familiar, so his letters were designed to imitate handwriting.
What happened between Gutenberg and Fust in 1455?
Fust took Gutenberg to court and took over much of the workshop.
Where does the terminology of upper case and lower case come from?
It comes from the wooden cases where printers kept their capital letters and small letters.
What point does the writer make lastly?
Lastly, the writer says that many people in China, Korea and Germany deserve credit for printing.

lessons.title: The Many Parents of the Light Bulb
lessons.summary: Davy, de la Rue, Swan, Edison and Lewis Latimer each helped bring electric light into homes.
lessons.text:
The light bulb is usually credited to Thomas Edison, yet electric light had many parents, and several of them deserve a share of the laurels.

The story starts in London in the early nineteenth century, when the chemist Humphry Davy made a brilliant arc of light leap between two pieces of carbon. It was far too bright, and too hungry for power, to use at home. In 1840, Warren de la Rue put a coil of platinum inside a glass tube from which the air had been removed, because without air the hot wire would not burn. His lamp worked, but platinum cost a fortune.

Midway through the century, the English chemist Joseph Swan began to experiment with thin strips of carbon in glass bulbs, and by early 1879 he was showing working lamps to audiences in the north of England.

Edison, in the United States, had a different advantage: money and people. In 1878, a syndicate of wealthy investors, including the banker J. P. Morgan, paid for his new electric light company. The syndicate expected results, and Edison's large team at Menlo Park, New Jersey, tested thousands of materials before a thread of carbon glowed for more than thirteen hours in October 1879. On the last night of that year, about 3,000 people came by train to see his laboratory lit up.

His team also designed the system around the bulb, from power stations and wires to a screw-in socket that is still used in much of the world. Without a socket that anyone could use, the bulb would have remained a laboratory toy.

Then came the legal fallout. Edison and Swan both claimed the invention, and the two heavy hitters of electric light jockeyed for position in court. Edison was the bigger hitter in the newspapers, but Swan had shown his lamps first. After some jockeying, they chose to join rather than fight, and in 1883 they formed a single company in Britain. The fallout turned into a partnership.

Swan had his own theatrical moment. In 1881, his lamps lit the Savoy Theatre in London, the first public building lit entirely by electricity. Gas lamps had made theaters hot and full of smoke, so the theatrical world welcomed the clean new light. Soon the change reached homes, and decor changed too: without smoke and flame, lighter colors and fabrics entered home decor.

One more name belongs here. Lewis Latimer, the son of parents who had escaped from slavery, taught himself technical drawing and in 1882 patented a better way to make the carbon threads inside bulbs. Midway through his career, he joined Edison's company as an expert in patent cases. He also wrote poems, which were collected in a book late in his life. In Latimer, a poetic side and a precise side lived together.

None of these inventors rested on his laurels, and none worked alone.

Questions:
Who paid for Edison's new electric light company?
A syndicate of wealthy investors, including the banker J. P. Morgan, paid for it.
Why was the screw-in socket important?
Without a socket that anyone could use, the bulb would have remained a laboratory toy.
How did the theatrical world react to Swan's lamps?
It welcomed the clean new light, because gas lamps had made theaters hot and full of smoke.
What did Lewis Latimer do besides his technical work?
He wrote poems, which shows that he had a poetic side as well as a precise one.

lessons.title: A Wooden Box in Dayton
lessons.summary: When their 1901 glider failed, the Wright brothers built a small wind tunnel and measured lift for themselves.
lessons.text:
In the fall of 1901, Wilbur and Orville Wright came home to Dayton, Ohio, in a gloomy mood. They ran a bicycle shop, and for two summers they had tested gliders on the windy sand hills of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The 1901 glider had been a disappointment. It produced only about a third of the lift that their calculations had promised, and in a strong gust the pilot felt almost helpless. On the train home, Wilbur said that people might not fly for a thousand years.

Lift is the upward push that air gives a wing, and to design a wing you need to know how much lift each shape will give. The brothers had taken their figures from published tables, especially those of Otto Lilienthal, the German pioneer who had died in a gliding crash in 1896. A sane engineer trusts published data until it fails, but the Wrights now faced a choice. They could revert to guesswork, or they could test the tables themselves. Many people thought that no sane person would try to fly at all.

They chose to test. Their deduction was simple: if the glider flew worse than the numbers predicted, then either the glider or the numbers were wrong. To find out which, they built a wind tunnel, a wooden box about 6 feet long, with a fan driven by the engine that powered their shop. Inside, moving air would collide with small model wings made of thin metal, and the force with which the air collided with each wing could be measured.

The brothers built delicate balances from old bicycle spokes and pieces of saw blade, and over about two months they tested some 200 wing shapes. It was slow, careful work, and it entailed thousands of readings.

The results led to a second deduction. An old number used in all lift calculations, more than a century old, was too large, so every result built on it had been affected negatively. Lilienthal's tables, meanwhile, described a wing unlike the Wrights' own, which also affected their results negatively.

With their new tables, the brothers built the 1902 glider, which flew beautifully. They made hundreds of flights in it and learned to control it, so that the pilot was no longer helpless in a sudden gust. They never had to revert to their old figures. On December 17, 1903, Orville flew their powered machine for 12 seconds, and the age of flight began.

The Wrights were dreamers, but their success came from realism, and their realism meant believing measurements more than hopes. They also had help. The engineer Octave Chanute shared his knowledge with them freely, and their mechanic, Charlie Taylor, built the engine.

Today, engineers test new aircraft in a computer simulator before any metal is cut, and pilots train in a flight simulator before they fly. Yet the method is the one the Wrights used in their wooden box: question the numbers, then measure.

Questions:
Why were the brothers disappointed with the 1901 glider?
It produced only about a third of the lift that they had expected, and the pilot felt almost helpless in a strong gust.
What was their first deduction?
If the glider flew worse than predicted, either the glider or the numbers were wrong.
What did the testing entail?
It entailed thousands of readings, each one written down by hand.
Where do engineers test new aircraft today?
They test them in a computer simulator before any metal is cut.

lessons.title: Hedy Lamarr's Jumping Signal
lessons.summary: The film star Hedy Lamarr and the composer George Antheil invented frequency hopping, an idea that was ignored for years.
lessons.text:
In her day, Hedy Lamarr was often called the most beautiful woman in the world. That label hid an intriguing fact: in her spare time she was an inventor, and an idea she helped to create lives on in some of our wireless devices.

Born Hedwig Kiesler in Vienna in 1914, she was a young actress when she married Fritz Mandl, a rich arms dealer who sold weapons to the dictatorship of Benito Mussolini in Italy. At his dinner table she listened quietly while engineers and officers discussed weapons, including torpedoes guided by radio. The marriage was unhappy, and in 1937 she escaped. After the breakup, she went to London and then to Hollywood. She was part of a great exodus of artists and scientists who left Europe as the dictatorship in Germany grew stronger, and that exodus brought the United States many of its finest minds.

In Hollywood she met George Antheil, a composer who loved machines, and together they took up a problem from those dinners. A torpedo guided by radio is easy to stop: the enemy simply finds the frequency and fills it with noise, which is called jamming. Her intriguing solution was to make the signal jump. If the sender and the torpedo changed frequency together, many times a second, following the same secret pattern, an enemy could never hold on to the signal. Antheil, who had once written music for several player pianos playing in perfect time, suggested rolls like piano rolls to keep the two sides together.

They received a patent in 1942 and offered it to the United States Navy. The Navy put it aside and suggested that she would help more by selling war bonds. At one fundraiser after another the turnout was enormous, because people wanted to see a film star in person, and she raised millions of dollars.

Here lies the paradox of her life. The beauty that made her famous also kept people from taking her ideas seriously. Then the patent was allowed to lapse before the idea was widely used, so she never earned anything from it. Only after that lapse did similar methods spread into military radio and then into everyday technology. Bluetooth headphones, for example, use frequency hopping, and related ideas helped shape early wireless broadband. Engineers still debate how much later broadband systems owe to her patent itself, but the family of ideas is the same.

In 2014, years after her death, she and Antheil were added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame. Her story has a special resonance today, because it reminds us that talent can hide behind a famous face. It also has resonance for anyone whose good idea came before the world was ready. Credit belongs to both partners: she brought the jump, and he brought the machine that kept time.

Questions:
What was her solution to jamming?
She made the signal jump between frequencies, following a secret pattern shared by the sender and the torpedo.
Why was the turnout at her fundraisers so large?
People wanted to see a film star in person, so the turnout at every fundraiser was enormous.
What did she do after the breakup of her marriage?
After the breakup, she went to London and then to Hollywood.
What is the paradox of her life?
The beauty that made her famous also kept people from taking her ideas seriously.

lessons.title: The Long Road to the Zipper
lessons.summary: Elias Howe, Whitcomb Judson and Gideon Sundback took sixty years to turn a clumsy fastener into the modern zipper.
lessons.text:
Few inventions are as ordinary as the zipper, and few took so long to work properly.

The first step came from Elias Howe, who is famous for his work on the sewing machine. In 1851 he patented a kind of continuous fastener for clothing, but sewing machines kept him busy and he never sold it. The idea slept for forty years.

In 1893, Whitcomb Judson, an inventor in Chicago, patented a "clasp locker", a chain of hooks and eyes that closed with a sliding piece. It was mostly meant for boots and shoes. People found it a pleasant novelty, but the novelty soon wore off, because the device had a habit of sticking or springing open at the worst moment. It could annoy customers more than ordinary laces did, and few things annoy a buyer more than a fastener that opens on its own.

The man who solved the problem was Gideon Sundback, an engineer born in Sweden who had moved to the United States. In 1906 he took a job at Judson's company, at first as a subordinate engineer. It might have been a short stint, but the stint lasted the rest of his working life. He married Elvira Aronson, the daughter of the plant manager, and they were happy together until she died in 1911. Many accounts say that, in his mourning, he found comfort in long hours at his drawing table, and that the months of mourning were also months of hard work.

By 1913 he had the answer. Instead of hooks and eyes, his fastener used rows of small metal teeth, each with a tiny cup on one side and a bump on the other, so that each tooth fitted into the next. A slider pressed the two rows together or pulled them apart. He also designed machines to make the teeth cheaply, which mattered just as much: an invention that cannot be made in large numbers rarely changes daily life. His career had a clear trajectory: from subordinate to head designer, and from a weak design to a reliable one.

Even then, the public was slow to accept it. Sewing a fastener into clothes needed new skills, and tailors trusted buttons. The name we use came later, in 1923, when the Goodrich company put the new fasteners on rubber boots. The sound they made was the giveaway: the company called the boots "Zippers", and the name soon stuck to the fastener itself.

From boots, the fastener moved to bags, then to children's clothes, because a child could dress without help, and finally to pants and jackets. Its trajectory from a novelty for shoes to a part of almost every jacket took about forty years.

Credit is shared here too. Howe had an early idea, Judson had the ambition, and Sundback, a modest engineer from Sweden, made it work.

Questions:
Why did Elias Howe never sell his fastener?
Sewing machines kept him busy, so he never sold it.
Why did people stop enjoying Judson's novelty?
The device had a habit of sticking or springing open, and it could annoy customers more than laces did.
How did Sundback's fastener work?
It used rows of small metal teeth that fitted into each other, and a slider pressed them together or pulled them apart.
Where did the name come from?
The sound of the fasteners on rubber boots was the giveaway, and the company called the boots "Zippers".

lessons.title: A Melted Candy Bar
lessons.summary: Percy Spencer noticed a melted candy bar near a radar tube, and the microwave oven slowly found its way into kitchens.
lessons.text:
Some inventions are planned for years. The microwave oven began with a sticky pocket.

Percy Spencer was born in Maine in 1894. His father died when he was very young, and he grew up with an aunt and uncle who had little money. Deprived of most schooling, he left school at about twelve to work in a mill. Yet a deprived childhood did not hold him back. He taught himself about electricity, learned radio in the Navy, and became one of the leading engineers at Raytheon, a company near Boston.

During the Second World War, Raytheon made magnetrons, the tubes that produce the radio waves for radar. A powerful new type of magnetron had been developed in Britain in 1940 by John Randall and Harry Boot, and Spencer found ways to build them in great numbers. One day in 1945, while he stood near a working magnetron, he noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted.

Other people had felt warmth near radar equipment, but Spencer was curious enough to test it. He placed some corn near the tube, and it popped. Then he tried an egg, which heated so fast that it burst, and the result was hardly edible. The waves, it turned out, made the water inside food move, and that movement produced heat.

Raytheon built the first microwave oven in 1947. It was nearly 6 feet tall, weighed about 750 pounds and cost thousands of dollars, so it went to restaurants, ships and trains rather than homes. A popular tabletop model did not arrive until 1967, when Amana, a company owned by Raytheon, sold one small enough for an ordinary kitchen. After that, the tabletop oven spread quickly.

It changed the way people treat a leftover. Last night's rice, a cold burger patty, a bowl of soup: each leftover could be warm and edible in two minutes. Cooks soon learned the oven's habits. A loose cover keeps food moist, because the steam stays inside. A frozen patty needs several short rounds so that it heats evenly. A doughnut warmed for ten seconds tastes almost fresh, but a doughnut warmed for a minute turns hard and chewy. A hot dog takes less than a minute, and the mustard goes on afterward, so the mustard stays cool and bright.

Waiting for the countdown on the door may be the least zen moment in the modern kitchen: we stand and watch the numbers fall, impatient with a machine that already saves us twenty minutes. A truly zen cook might use those ninety seconds simply to breathe.

Spencer received many patents and much respect, though little money from the oven, because Raytheon owned his work. Still, every time a countdown ends with a beep, his curious pocket is part of the story, along with Randall, Boot and the many engineers who made the oven small and safe.

Questions:
Why did Percy Spencer leave school early?
He grew up poor and was deprived of most schooling, so he left at about twelve to work in a mill.
Why did the first microwave oven go to restaurants, ships and trains?
It was nearly 6 feet tall, weighed about 750 pounds and cost thousands of dollars.
How can you keep a leftover moist in the oven?
You can use a loose cover, because the steam stays inside.
Why is waiting for the countdown not a zen moment?
We stand and watch the numbers fall, impatient with a machine that already saves us time.

lessons.title: Grace Hopper Teaches Computers English
lessons.summary: From Jacquard's punched cards to Grace Hopper's first compiler and COBOL, programming moved closer to human language.
lessons.text:
In 1804, Joseph Marie Jacquard, the son of a weaver in Lyon, built a loom controlled by cards with holes punched in them. Each card told the loom which threads to lift, so the machine could weave a complicated pattern again and again without a mistake. A weaver no longer had to remember the pattern; the cards remembered it. The idea of a machine that follows stored instructions later inspired the first designs for computers, and it was still at work when Grace Hopper began her career.

Hopper was a mathematician who taught at Vassar College. In 1943, during the war, she joined the United States Navy, and the following year she was sent to Harvard to work on the Mark I, a machine 51 feet long that could compute tables for the Navy's guns. Programming it was exhausting. Every instruction had to be written as numbers, punched into tape and checked by hand, and one wrong digit could ruin hours of work.

After the war, Hopper moved to a company that was building the UNIVAC, one of the first computers sold to businesses. She noticed that programmers kept writing the same pieces of code again and again. Why not keep the useful pieces in a library and let the computer find and combine them itself? In 1952, her team produced a program called A-0, often described as the first compiler: a program that turns instructions written by people into the numbers a machine can compute with.

Her larger dream was a language close to English. Many experts said that computers could only do arithmetic. Hopper's confidence overrode their doubts. Her team built FLOW-MATIC, which accepted commands made of English words, and it became one of the main models for COBOL, a business language designed in 1959 by a committee of experts from industry and government. Hopper advised that committee, and other people, such as the programmer Jean Sammet, played central roles.

Building such a language meant thinking about semantics, the study of meaning. A word like "add" has to mean exactly one thing to the machine. Hopper understood that semantic clarity, more than cleverness, was what made a program readable by the next person who opened it.

COBOL spread through banks, insurance companies and governments, and many organizations developed a deep dependency on it. Some of that code still runs today. Modern programmers keep their code in an online repository and list each dependency their program needs, but the basic arrangement, a library of reusable parts and a compiler that joins them, is the one Hopper argued for.

She stayed in the Navy until she was 79 and retired as a rear admiral. She liked to warn young officers that habit should never override common sense, and she handed them pieces of wire about 1 foot long to show how far light travels in a billionth of a second. Like Jacquard's cards, her small gifts carried large ideas.

Questions:
What did Jacquard's cards do?
Each card told the loom which threads to lift, so the machine could weave a pattern without a mistake.
What is a compiler?
It is a program that turns instructions written by people into the numbers a machine can compute with.
Why did semantics matter to Hopper?
A word like "add" has to mean exactly one thing, and semantic clarity makes a program readable.
Where do modern programmers keep their code?
They keep it in an online repository and list each dependency their program needs.

lessons.title: The Humble Steel Box
lessons.summary: Malcom McLean, Keith Tantlinger and many others turned the shipping container into the quiet engine of world trade.
lessons.text:
Look at any freeway near a port, and you will see trucks pulling long steel boxes. The shipping container is so ordinary that we hardly notice it, yet it changed the world economy as much as almost any invention of the last century.

Before the container, cargo moved piece by piece. Sacks, barrels and crates were carried onto ships by teams of dock workers, packed by hand and unpacked by hand at the other end. A ship could spend a week in port. The old ports lay along the riverside in cities such as New York, where piers ran out into the water, and whole riverside neighborhoods lived on this work.

Malcom McLean, a trucking businessman from North Carolina, thought the method wasted time and money. Why lift a thousand separate items when you could lift one box? On April 26, 1956, a converted tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, to Houston with 58 containers on board. Loading it cost a small fraction of what loading loose cargo did, and trucks could carry the boxes straight from the ship to the freeway.

McLean did not design everything himself. The engineer Keith Tantlinger developed strong corner fittings and a twist lock, a simple device that joins one container to another or to a truck. McLean later released those patents so that a single international standard could be built on them. Port planners, crane designers and the governments that agreed on standard sizes also played a part.

The container also proved itself in military procurement. During the Vietnam War, the United States military struggled with chaotic supply lines, and McLean's ships began carrying goods across the Pacific in containers. That procurement contract showed how well the system worked over long distances, and the ships, rather than return empty, began to carry goods from Japan.

Because a container stays sealed until it arrives, the incidence of theft fell sharply, and so did the incidence of damage. Insured cargo became cheaper to ship, since an insured box was far less likely to arrive half empty.

Not all of the changes were welcome. Work moved from the old piers to huge new ports with space for cranes and trucks, and thousands of dock jobs disappeared. Containers also carry unwanted passengers: insects and seeds hidden in or on the boxes, some of which become invasive species in their new homes. Inspectors around the world now check containers for invasive pests.

When a container finally retires, it often finds a second life. You may see one parked in a driveway as a storage shed, or turned into a small café in a city courtyard. Old containers stacked beside railroad tracks often wear bright graffiti, and some cities even invite artists to paint graffiti on them. A box in a courtyard or on a driveway may look humble, but it has probably crossed oceans many times.

Questions:
How did cargo move before the container?
It moved piece by piece, carried onto ships by dock workers and packed and unpacked by hand.
What happened on April 26, 1956?
The Ideal X sailed from Newark to Houston with 58 containers on board.
Why did the incidence of theft fall?
A container stays sealed until it arrives, so thieves could not reach the goods.
What can happen to a container after it retires?
It can become a storage shed in a driveway or a small café in a city courtyard.

lessons.title: The Long Chase After Cold
lessons.summary: From cellars and ice houses to the ice trade, refrigerators, Birdseye's quick freezing and vaccine freezers.
lessons.text:
For most of history, keeping food cold meant finding a place where the cold already was. Families dug a cellar under the house, because the earth stays cool in summer, to store potatoes, apples and milk. In many old houses, a recess in the cellar wall, deep and shaded, held the butter, and a second recess held the cheese. Cold was something people borrowed from the ground or from the winter.

In the deserts of ancient Persia, builders made tall ice houses with domed roofs. On winter nights, water froze in shallow pools behind high walls, and workers cut the ice and stored it in deep pits under the domes, where it lasted into the summer.

In the early nineteenth century, a businessman from Boston named Frederic Tudor turned winter into a product. Workers cut blocks of ice from the lakes of New England, packed them in sawdust and shipped them to the Caribbean and even to India. Customers paid for purity as well as cold: clear ice from a clean lake was worth more than cloudy ice from a dirty river. Worries about purity grew as cities expanded, because ice cut from polluted water could carry disease.

John Gorrie, a doctor in Florida, wanted to cool the rooms of patients suffering from fever, and in 1851 he patented a machine that made ice. Doctors had long used ice to bring down fevers and to reduce swelling, and Gorrie hoped that cool air would help his patients recover. He never found investors. Others worked on the same problem, from Jacob Perkins in London, years before Gorrie, to Carl von Linde in Germany, decades after him.

Early in the twentieth century, the electric refrigerator began to enter homes. Early models used dangerous gases, and the safer ones that replaced them turned out, decades later, to harm the upper atmosphere, so in 1987 the world agreed to stop using them.

Meanwhile, Clarence Birdseye had noticed something in Labrador, in northern Canada. There, the Inuit froze fish in the bitter cold, and months later the fish tasted almost fresh. Birdseye realized that fast freezing forms tiny ice crystals that do little damage, while slow freezing forms large ones that ruin the texture. He developed machines for quick freezing, and frozen vegetables and fish entered the stores. Later, the home freezer let families conserve food for months, and to conserve energy, modern refrigerators use far better insulation than early ones.

During the COVID pandemic, some vaccines had to be stored at about minus 70 degrees Celsius, and hospitals rushed to buy special freezers. The pandemic showed that a cold chain, a series of refrigerators and freezers from factory to patient, matters as much as a road.

Today we still keep an ice pack in the freezer for a twisted ankle, to bring down the swelling, much as people once fetched ice from the cellar.

Questions:
Why did families store food in a cellar?
The earth stays cool in summer, so food kept longer in a cellar.
Why did Tudor's customers care about purity?
Clear ice from a clean lake was worth more, and ice from polluted water could carry disease.
What did Birdseye learn in Labrador?
He learned that fast freezing keeps fish almost fresh, because it forms tiny ice crystals.
What did the pandemic show about cold?
It showed that a cold chain of refrigerators and freezers matters as much as a road.

lessons.title: Inventions Without Inventors
lessons.summary: Fire, glue, beads, the canoe, irrigation and grafting were invented long before anyone wrote down a name.
lessons.text:
Many important inventions have no famous name attached to them. They were made long before writing and improved by thousands of people over thousands of years.

Our early ancestors lived on the African savanna, a wide, open land of grass and scattered trees. Life on the savanna was dangerous after dark, and fire changed that. People first used natural fires and later learned to make their own. Making fire needs tinder, a dry material that catches a spark easily, such as dry grass, bark or a certain kind of fungus. The famous Iceman found in the Alps, who died about 5,300 years ago, carried tinder in a small bag on his belt, ready to start a fire.

Fire made another invention possible: glue. Trees produce sap, and some trees, such as pines, give off a thick, sticky resin when their bark is cut. Neanderthals in Europe heated birch bark at least 200,000 years ago to make a dark tar, and they used it to fix stone points to wooden handles. Later people mixed pine resin with ash and other materials to make strong glues. Sticky sap and a hot fire, combined with patience, became a technology.

People also wanted beauty. Small shell beads with holes for a string have been found in Africa and the Middle East, some about 100,000 years old. These beads were probably worn as ornaments, perhaps to show who belonged to which group. An ornament has no practical use, which is exactly why it tells us so much: the people who wore it thought about how others saw them.

The oldest boat yet discovered is a canoe found in the Netherlands, dug out of a single pine trunk around 8000 BC. It is only about 10 feet long, but a canoe like it could carry a hunter across lakes and along rivers.

When people began to farm, water became the great problem. In Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and the Euphrates, farmers dug channels to bring river water to their fields. Irrigation let them grow food on dry land, but it was hard work, because the rivers could flood without warning. In the old stories of that region, floods were often described as the wrath of the gods, and irrigation was partly a way of living with that wrath.

Farmers also learned to graft. To graft a tree, you join a branch from one tree onto the roots of another, so that the new tree produces the same fruit as the first. Ancient farmers grafted apples and olives this way, and it is still the main way to grow good fruit trees. Early forestry grew from similar knowledge: people in ancient Britain cut certain trees near the ground so that many straight new stems would grow, providing wood for generations. Modern forestry still uses this method in some places.

No patent office records these inventions. They are the shared work of us all.

Questions:
What is tinder?
Tinder is a dry material that catches a spark easily, such as dry grass, bark or a certain fungus.
What did Neanderthals make from birch bark?
They heated it to make a dark tar and used it to fix stone points to wooden handles.
Why were shell beads probably worn?
They were probably worn as ornaments, perhaps to show who belonged to which group.
What does it mean to graft a tree?
It means to join a branch from one tree onto the roots of another.
